setup: A USD 1m equity portfolio is tracked against an index. Over one year the portfolio grows to USD 1.12m, while the index rises from 2000 to 2180 points. Tracking error is 4%.
ask: The portfolio's active return (alpha) for the year is:

options.label: -3 percentage points
options.why: Subtracted the wrong way round (benchmark minus portfolio). The portfolio beat its index, so active return is positive.

options.label: +12 percentage points
options.why: Used the portfolio's own return and forgot to take off the benchmark's 9%.

options.label: +21 percentage points
options.why: Added the two returns (12% + 9%) instead of subtracting them.

takeaway: Active return is portfolio minus benchmark, both as percentage returns. Index points must be turned into a return first.

setup: A portfolio's excess returns are regressed on the benchmark's excess returns (60 observations). Portfolio average excess return 3.29%, benchmark average excess return 0.98%, slope 1.5237. The raw active return is $3.29 - 0.98 = 2.31\%$.

options.label: Equal to 2.31%
options.why: Treated the slope as 1, which turns alpha back into the raw active return. The slope here is 1.52, so the benchmark must be scaled up.

options.label: Above 2.31%
options.why: Added $\beta \times 0.98\%$ to the portfolio's return instead of subtracting it (giving about 4.8%).

takeaway: Alpha strips out the beta-scaled benchmark return. With beta above 1 and a positive benchmark, it lands below the raw active return. The numerator of the IR is alpha, not the raw difference.

setup: For 2017 a fund averaged a 32% return with beta 1.15. The market averaged 25% and the T-bill rate was 6%.
ask: The return that the fund's beta justifies under CAPM is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied beta by the market premium (19%) but left out the 6% T-bill rate.
Applied beta to the whole market return (25%) instead of the premium over the T-bill rate.
Ignored beta and used the market return as the benchmark. At beta 1.15 the justified return is higher.

takeaway: Benchmark-adjust with $r_f + \beta(R_m - r_f)$, then alpha is actual minus that. Apply beta to the premium only.

setup: A fund returned 11% in a year. The risk-free rate was 3% and the S&P 500 returned 9%. The regression beta to the S&P 500 is 0.80 and the tracking error is 5%. A naive comparison with the raw index gives $(11 - 9)/5 = 0.40$.
ask: Measured against the beta-adjusted benchmark, the information ratio is:

options.label: Lower than 0.40
options.why: Assumed that adjusting for beta can only shrink alpha. With beta below 1 the benchmark is expected to earn less than 9%, so alpha grows.

options.label: The same, 0.40
options.why: Ignored the beta of 0.80 and kept the raw index as the benchmark.

takeaway: A beta below 1 lowers the benchmark return that the fund is expected to earn, so alpha and the IR rise against the beta-adjusted benchmark.

setup: Over five years a manager's active returns (portfolio minus benchmark, in %) were $+0.2,\ -0.2,\ +0.5,\ 0.0,\ +1.5$. The mean is $+0.40\%$. Tracking error is the sample standard deviation of these active returns.
ask: Is the information ratio (mean active return / tracking error) above or below 1?

options.label: Above 1
options.why: Treated the 0.40% mean as larger than the spread. The 1.5% year alone sits 1.1 points from the mean, so the standard deviation (0.67%) exceeds 0.40%.

takeaway: The IR is below 1 whenever the tracking error exceeds the mean active return. The betas in the table play no part.

setup: A firm lets each manager make at most 100 independent transactions (bets) a year. One manager wants an information ratio of 0.75. Use the fundamental law, $IR = IC \times \sqrt{BR}$.
ask: The information coefficient she needs is closest to:

options.why: Set IC equal to the IR, ignoring breadth altogether.
Divided by $BR = 100$ instead of by $\sqrt{100} = 10$.
Multiplied by $\sqrt{BR}$ instead of dividing. An IC above 1 is impossible.

takeaway: Breadth enters under a square root, so 100 bets cut the skill needed by a factor of 10, not 100.

setup: A fund targets an IR of 0.60 and uses the fundamental law with $TC = 1$. Analyst 1 would place 250 independent bets a year; Analyst 2 only 25.
ask: To just reach the target, which analyst needs the higher information coefficient?

options.label: Analyst 1 (250 bets)
options.why: Read more bets as demanding more skill. Breadth and skill trade off: with more bets, each can be less accurate.

options.label: Both the same
options.why: Overlooked that $IC = IR/\sqrt{BR}$ falls as breadth rises. The target is the same, the breadth is not.

takeaway: Fewer bets mean each must be better: for the same IR, required IC is inversely proportional to $\sqrt{BR}$.

setup: A quant fund forecasts alphas every month across a 3,000-stock universe, making 25 independent forecasts each month. Its model has an information coefficient of 0.15.
ask: The annual information ratio is closest to:

options.why: Used a single month's breadth (25) and never annualised: $0.15 \times \sqrt{25}$.
Used the 3,000-stock universe as breadth ($0.15 \times \sqrt{3000}$). Only independent forecasts count.
Combined both errors: 3,000 stocks times 12 months as breadth ($0.15 \times \sqrt{36000}$).

takeaway: Breadth is the number of independent bets per year, not the universe size: annualise by multiplying the monthly count by 12.

setup: A company runs three independent, equally weighted active strategies. Each has an expected alpha of 5% and a tracking error of 8.4%, so each has the same IR.
ask: Compared with one manager's IR, the combined IR is:

options.label: Above one manager's IR but below three times it
Three times one manager's IR
options.why: Added the IRs linearly. That holds only for perfectly correlated strategies; independent ones combine as $\sqrt{3}$.

options.label: Equal to one manager's IR
options.why: Averaged the three strategies and ignored the diversification gain from independence.

takeaway: Independent equal-IR strategies combine as $IR\sqrt{N}$: better than one, well short of $N$ times.

setup: A fund holds Goodman and HiEdge, whose returns are uncorrelated. The whole portfolio's annual 95% VaR is USD 7.2m and Goodman's alone is USD 5m.

options.label: About USD 2.2m
options.why: Subtracted the VaRs ($7.2 - 5$). That treats them as adding linearly, which holds only at correlation 1.

options.label: Above USD 7.2m
options.why: With zero correlation the portfolio VaR is the root of the sum of squares, so it exceeds each part. HiEdge alone cannot exceed the total.

takeaway: At zero correlation VaRs add in quadrature: the missing leg is $\sqrt{\text{total}^2 - \text{known}^2}$, slightly above the known one when the total is only modestly larger.

setup: A USD 100m portfolio P has 10% annual volatility. A manager considers adding a USD 40m position A with 20% annual volatility; the correlation of A with P is 0.5. Normal returns, 95% confidence, $z = 1.65$.
ask: Which is larger: A's incremental VaR (full revaluation, with and without A) or A's standalone VaR?

options.label: Incremental VaR
options.why: Expected the added position to raise portfolio VaR by more than its own VaR. With correlation below 1, diversification means the increase is smaller.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: Assumed correlation of 1, where VaRs add exactly. At 0.5 there is a diversification gain.

takeaway: Incremental VaR never exceeds standalone VaR for a normal portfolio: it equals it only at correlation 1.

setup: A USD 200m portfolio holds USD 18m of Alphabet. Annual volatilities: Alphabet 22%, portfolio 27%. The correlation between Alphabet and the portfolio is 0.54. Normal returns, 99% VaR with $z = 2.33$.
ask: Alphabet's beta to the portfolio, $\rho\sigma_A/\sigma_P$, is closest to:

options.why: Used the correlation as the beta. Beta also scales by the ratio of volatilities.
Inverted the volatility ratio ($\rho\sigma_P/\sigma_A$).
Dropped the correlation and used only $\sigma_A/\sigma_P$.

takeaway: Beta to the portfolio is $\rho \times \sigma_{asset}/\sigma_{portfolio}$; the asset's own volatility goes on top, the portfolio's underneath.

setup: Two airline stocks, annual volatilities: Venus USD 450m at 16%, Mars USD 250m at 11%. The USD 700m portfolio has volatility 14%. Use 95% confidence with $z = 1.645$.
ask: The diversification benefit (undiversified VaR minus diversified VaR) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 161m
options.why: Reported the diversified VaR itself ($1.645 \times 0.14 \times 700$) instead of the difference.

options.label: ≈ USD 25m
options.why: Scale slip (10 times): the two VaRs are both about 162, and their gap is 2.5, not 25.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.25m
options.why: Scale slip (1/10): the gap between 163.7 and 161.2 is 2.5.

takeaway: When the portfolio volatility (14%) is almost the weighted average of the parts (14.2%), the diversification benefit is tiny.

setup: A portfolio holds USD 2.5m of asset A (volatility 6%, beta to the portfolio 0.97) and USD 1.0m of asset B (volatility 10%, beta 1.075). A is 71.4% of portfolio value.
ask: A's share of portfolio VaR (component VaR / portfolio VaR) is:

options.label: Above 71.4%
options.why: Let the larger position dominate the risk. The share is weight times beta, and A's beta is below 1.

options.label: Exactly 71.4%
options.why: Used the weight alone and ignored beta, which measures how much each position loads on the portfolio's risk.

takeaway: Share of portfolio VaR is weight times beta. A beta below 1 puts the share below the weight, and the shares always sum to 100%.

setup: An FX portfolio holds USD 26m in sterling and USD 40m in lira. Betas to the portfolio: sterling 0.80, lira 1.13. The diversified portfolio VaR is USD 7m.
ask: The component VaR of the sterling position is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.085m
options.why: Stopped at the marginal VaR per dollar ($7/66 \times 0.80 = 0.085$) and read it as a dollar figure.

options.label: ≈ USD 5.6m
options.why: Multiplied portfolio VaR by the beta ($7 \times 0.80$) and left out the position's weight.

options.label: ≈ USD 21m
options.why: Took position times beta ($26 \times 0.80$) with no VaR-to-value scaling, so the result is not a VaR at all.

takeaway: Component VaR = marginal VaR per dollar times the position. Check it is well below the total VaR of 7m before trusting it.

setup: Portfolio X has a VaR of USD 100,000 and holds five equally weighted assets A to E. Asset C has a beta of 1.5. Its pro-rata share of VaR would be USD 20,000.

options.label: Below USD 20,000
options.why: Treated the high beta as a diversifier. A beta above 1 means C adds more than its weight to portfolio risk.

options.label: Exactly USD 20,000
options.why: Ignored beta and split the VaR equally across five assets.

takeaway: Component VaR = portfolio VaR times weight times beta, so beta above 1 puts it above the pro-rata share.

setup: A USD 1m portfolio holds USD 300,000 in A (daily volatility 3%) and USD 700,000 in B (daily volatility 5%). The correlation between A and B is 0.4. The dollar volatilities are USD 9,000 and USD 35,000.
ask: The portfolio's 1-day dollar standard deviation lies:

options.label: Below USD 35,000
options.why: Expected diversification to push risk below the bigger leg. That needs negative correlation; even at zero correlation the total is about 36,100.

options.label: Above USD 44,000
options.why: Went beyond the perfect-correlation ceiling ($9,000 + 35,000 = 44,000$), for instance by leaving the square root off the variance.

takeaway: Portfolio volatility sits between the root-sum-of-squares (zero correlation) and the straight sum (correlation 1); a positive correlation puts it in that band above the larger leg.

setup: A portfolio of four equal positions of USD 10m has a VaR of USD 8m. Burki Refinery's beta to the portfolio is 1.4.
ask: Burki's marginal VaR (VaR change per dollar invested) is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied by the 25% weight as well, double-counting the position size.
Divided VaR by a single USD 10m position instead of the USD 40m portfolio.
Multiplied VaR by beta ($8 \times 1.4$) and never divided by portfolio value.

takeaway: Marginal VaR = (portfolio VaR / portfolio value) times beta. It is per dollar, so a number near 0.3, not millions.

setup: Two perfectly correlated assets: A is USD 2.5m with 6% volatility, B is USD 1.0m with 10% volatility. Use $z = 1.65$ (95%).
ask: Which asset has the larger individual 95% VaR?

options.label: Asset B
options.why: Compared volatilities alone. A's position is 2.5 times B's, which outweighs B's higher percentage volatility.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: Thought perfect correlation equalises the two. Correlation affects the portfolio VaR only, not an asset's own VaR.

takeaway: Individual VaR = position times z times volatility; size matters as much as volatility, and correlation is irrelevant at this stage.
